nameStory: Leccinum longicurvipes gets its scientific name from the Latin 'longus' meaning long and 'curvipes' meaning curved foot, referring to its distinctively long, often curved stem. While it lacks a widely-used common name, mycologists sometimes call it the Long-stemmed Scaber Stalk, highlighting its most obvious feature.
description: This is a medium to large bolete mushroom with pores instead of gills under its cap. It typically has a brownish to reddish-brown cap that can reach 4-6 inches across, sitting atop an unusually long stem that can stretch 6-8 inches tall. The stem is covered in dark, rough scales called scabers that give it a distinctly textured appearance, and the whole mushroom has a sturdy, substantial feel when you handle it.

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Exceptionally long stem, often 6-8 inches tall, covered in dark brown to blackish rough scales (scabers) that feel gritty to the touch. The stem may appear slightly curved and is typically white underneath the scales.

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Brownish to reddish-brown cap, 3-6 inches across, with a slightly sticky or tacky surface when moist. The cap feels firm and spongy, with a texture like a dinner roll.

idTips.label: Pores
idTips.description: Tiny white to cream-colored pores under the cap instead of gills, like a natural sponge. They may bruise yellowish or brownish when pressed gently with your finger.

idTips.label: Bruising
idTips.description: Cut flesh typically turns pinkish to wine-red, then darkens to black or blue-black over several minutes. This color change is quite dramatic and distinctive.

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Pleasant, mild mushroomy smell with no unpleasant or chemical odors. Some describe it as slightly nutty or earthy when fresh.

habitat: Found in mixed and deciduous forests throughout New England, typically growing near birch, aspen, or other hardwood trees in a beneficial partnership with their roots. Look for it in rich, moist soil along forest edges, trails, and clearings, especially in areas with good drainage. It's most common at lower to mid elevations and seems to prefer spots that get dappled sunlight.

seasonality.spring: Not typically found in spring, though mycelium (the underground fungal network) is actively growing and preparing for summer fruiting.
seasonality.summer: Peak season begins in mid to late summer, especially after warm rains. Fresh specimens are firm and have the best color contrast between cap and stem.
seasonality.fall: Continues fruiting into early fall, though specimens may be more weathered. Look for newer flushes after September rains.
seasonality.winter: No active fruiting; mushrooms from fall may persist as dried, blackened remnants on the forest floor.

funFact: This mushroom can actually pump water up through its incredibly long stem like a natural drinking straw, sometimes moving moisture from deep soil layers up to the cap - a feat that would be like you drinking through a straw taller than a basketball hoop!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other Leccinum species like the Brown Birch Bolete, but this species' exceptionally long stem (often twice as long as similar boletes) and dramatic bruising reaction help distinguish it. Remember: "Long name, long stem" - if the stem seems unusually tall for a bolete, you're likely looking at longicurvipes.
contextualKnowledge: The genus name Leccinum comes from an old Italian word for a type of bolete, and all members of this genus form beneficial partnerships with tree roots. These partnerships are so specific that identifying the nearby trees can actually help confirm which Leccinum species you've found.
compareHints: Among its Leccinum relatives, this species stands out for having the longest, most elongated stem - often appearing almost comically stretched compared to the Red-capped Scaber Stalk or Brown Birch Bolete. While other Leccinum species typically have stems 3-5 inches tall, longicurvipes regularly exceeds 6 inches and may curve noticeably. The dramatic flesh bruising to wine-red then black is also more pronounced than in most of its cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Leccinum relatives, this species stands out for its intensely red-orange cap color - the Orange Birch Bolete is more yellow-orange, while the Brown Birch-bolete is brownish.
